# Jacob Dutton

> Jacob Dutton uses AI for value creation, growth and innovation. He gets AI working for large companies, groups and investors: figuring out where it pays, proving it works and scaling what does. Based in Abu Dhabi, UAE. Former SVP Innovation, R&D and Emerging Technology at ADQ, the Abu Dhabi sovereign investor, where he managed the $150M portfolio innovation fund across 20+ operating companies. Currently Global Head of AI Innovation at Aucctus AI.

Jacob decides which AI use cases get funded, proves they work before they scale and gets them into day-to-day work. The CIO, CTO and CISO own platforms, data, security and model risk, and nothing gets funded that can't clear their bar. He has put most kinds of AI to work: predictive models, computer vision and physical AI, generative AI, and agents connected to a company's own systems and data. Each one is tested with evals before and after launch, with guardrails and a person signing off where it matters. Roles his work fits: Chief AI Officer, head of AI value creation, portfolio value creation, chief innovation officer.

## What he does

- Value creation: where AI will save or make the most money in the business a company already runs. He works out which AI use cases are worth funding, tests them on the company's own data and real cases, and stops the ones that don't work early. At ADQ, 16 AI initiatives were funded for $33M, with $40M+ of first-year savings.
- Growth: where AI can grow what a company already sells. He finds where AI lifts revenue in existing products, services and channels and gets it in front of customers, from machine learning on product data to generative AI that personalises at scale, for Fortune 100 clients inside an NYSE-listed holding company and for businesses like Hilton, JCB and Walgreens. Example: AI predictive maintenance built into JCB's heavy equipment.
- Innovation: net new AI-powered ventures, products and services, from the first test with customers to a business that makes money. Done inside IPG, through Future Foundry for clients like Mars, Microsoft and Salesforce, and in his own venture studio. 10 businesses launched at IPG, one to $20M ARR in 18 months.

## Point of view: AI should be funded like a portfolio, not a project

Most companies fund AI as a project: pick a use case, build it, roll it out and hope people use it. That's why so much stalls after the pilot. Jacob runs it as a portfolio instead: five stages, and the money only grows as the evidence does. He calls it the Traction Method, because what counts is AI in use and paying back.

1. Mine (no money yet): where could AI change the work? He runs sessions inside the business with the people who do the work, workflow by workflow, using their own process maps and their list of what's slow, costly or goes wrong. 276 AI opportunities were found this way across ADQ's operating companies.
2. Size (no money yet): what's it worth, and is it ready? Before a use case gets any money, it has to pass four checks. They put a value on it and name the assumption most likely to be wrong.
   - Worth: what the work costs today, and what doing it better is worth.
   - Ready: whether the data exists, is good enough and can be reached.
   - Standard: whether AI can do it as well as the best team does now.
   - Shared: whether it can be built once and reused across the group.
3. Test (a little money): does it work on our data? A little money pays for the cheapest test of that assumption, on the company's own data and real cases. Three things are agreed before it starts.
   - Owner: a named person in the business who answers for the result.
   - Baseline: what today's process costs, and how often it's right.
   - Target: the accuracy it has to hit on the company's own cases.
4. Prove (more money): does it pay in live work? If it passes the test, more money pays for a run in live work, measured against the baseline.
   - Supervised: a person checks the AI's work until it hits the target.
   - Cleared: signed off by the CIO, CTO and CISO before it goes live.
   - Measured: on cost per correct outcome, against the old way.
5. Scale (the most money): where else does it apply? Only what's proved gets the big money: the rollout, then reuse across teams, business units and group companies, so the second costs far less than the first. 16 of 276 made it this far at ADQ, from 100+ that went through three gates. All 16 are in use, with $40M+ of first-year savings.

Every use case is measured the same way: a baseline before it starts, the impact after, and one report across the portfolio.

## Point of view: where this ends up

Over the next decade, AI will push the cost of thinking, and then of doing, towards zero. Here's what that changes for investors, companies and customers.

- Investors: value moves from labour to capital, and from the company to the portfolio. As agents take on more of the work, what a business earns depends less on headcount and more on what it owns: its data, its customers and its right to act on them. The diligence question becomes how much of a company's work agents can do, and who keeps the margin when they do. Owners who fund AI across their companies as one portfolio, and share what works, will see returns build faster than those who leave each company to work it out alone.
- Companies: when everyone runs the same models, the models stop being an advantage. The advantage moves to a company's own data, what it knows about its customers, its distribution and the record of what's worked. Companies that wire that into their agents, with clear rules on what agents can decide alone, will pull ahead of competitors using the same tools. Org charts flatten and more of the company runs like a fund, backing small investments and scaling what works.
- Customers: customers will buy through agents, whether they're consumers or businesses. More buying will be done by agents, for consumers and for companies' procurement teams, comparing, choosing and reordering. Products have to be readable by machines, through APIs, as well as by people and their agents. Services move from billing by the hour or per user to payment on outcomes, and a brand matters most when a customer's agent has to decide who to trust.

## What he's built

AI-led ventures and products, each built with a large company on board from day one:

- CareFlow: Predicts when a hospital patient is deteriorating, from vital signs, lab results and clinical notes, so care teams can step in earlier. With Kaiser Permanente.
- LiveLink+: Built on top of JCB LiveLink. AI on machine data that predicts when heavy equipment needs maintenance, before it breaks down on site. With JCB.
- Jingzi: An AI personalisation engine for Avon in China, combining connected devices, biometric data and machine learning, sold as a WeChat skincare subscription. With Avon.
- CarbonOS: Automates carbon accounting across a supply chain by plugging into procurement and logistics data, with reports that stand up to audit. With BP.
- RegIntel: Reads regulatory changes, checks them against a firm's own policies and drafts the compliance reporting. With Grant Thornton.
- Twin: Digital twins of factory operations that predict failures before they happen and cut unplanned downtime. With Boeing.
- RouteLogic: Routes urban deliveries across vans, EVs and cargo bikes in real time, using live traffic, weather and demand. With GXO.
- Healthbox: AI-personalised supplements, formulated to each customer's own needs; 20,000+ subscribers, with renewals 35% above the category. With Holland & Barrett.

## Selected work

- Aucctus AI (2026 to now), Global Head of AI Innovation: Aucctus is an AI system for strategy, growth and innovation work in large companies, built on a memory of the company that learns from every test and decision. Its agents work inside each client's own systems, with people approving what matters. Jacob leads how enterprise clients get started: mapping their work, deciding where AI will pay back first, and getting it running on their own data, typically within four weeks of the first session.
- ADQ (2025 to 2026), SVP Innovation, R&D and Emerging Technology: set the function up to run AI-first, with generative AI and agents doing the opportunity mapping, screening and valuation, across a $300B sovereign investor and 20+ operating companies in aviation, energy, ports, logistics, food and healthcare. Managed the $150M portfolio innovation fund: 276 opportunities across the portfolio, 16 funded for $33M against evidence at each stage. Designed and led the Robotics Ramp-Up Programme across 19 operating companies: 23 pilots launched, 100+ robotics and physical AI partners brought in, across computer vision, autonomous mobile robots and inspection drones. Reviewed innovation capability across 13 operating companies and turned it into a three-horizon roadmap.
- Curzon Street Ventures (2023 to 2025), co-founder and CEO: place-based venture studio turning the operational problems of large companies into AI-led startups. Six ventures validated with corporate partners Kaiser Permanente, BP, Grant Thornton, Boeing, GXO and HSBC. $500,000 of corporate sponsorship, 25 corporate partners.
- Future Foundry (2021 to 2025), co-founder and CEO: business experimentation company. 500+ projects tested and 50+ launched, a 90% launch success rate, and more than $1bn of spend stopped on ideas that weren't going to work. Built the testing method used inside Salesforce, Microsoft, HSBC, Mars and Hilton.
- Interpublic Group (2018 to 2021), Managing Director, Innovation, New York: built IPG's first innovation and venture practice to 50 people. 10 businesses launched; three raised $45M of Series A between them and one reached $20M ARR in 18 months. AI products in market since 2018, including predictive maintenance for JCB and AI-personalised skincare for Avon China.
- 383 (2009 to 2018), employee number one to Managing Partner: grew a Birmingham product studio to 40+ people. Built the first Hive connected thermostat for British Gas, an $11M subscription business in year one.
- Maven (2021 to 2025), Expert Instructor, AI and Innovation Management: 200+ senior operators taught.
- Also: Advisory Board Member, Connected Places Catapult.

Career in four eras: 2009 to 2018, before AI, connected products and digital services (383); 2018 to 2021, AI in the product, machine learning, IoT and personalisation (IPG); 2021 to 2025, AI-assisted, generative AI and LLMs (Future Foundry, Curzon Street Ventures, Maven); 2025 to now, AI-native, agents and physical AI (ADQ, Aucctus AI).

Clients and organisations he has worked with include Microsoft, Salesforce, HSBC, Boeing, BP, Mars, P&G, Unilever, Reckitt, Kimberly-Clark, Novartis, Walgreens, Capital One, Experian, Ørsted, Hilton, JCB and the USPS.
